commitResults.messageTitle: Rename main class to GOAT and add greeting
Add Task subclasses and todo/deadline/event commands
Add custom exception and handle input errors
Update README for GOAT and acknowledge AI use
Add Storage class to save tasks to disk
commitResults.messageBody:
GOAT kept the task list only in memory, so everything the user entered
was lost when the program exited. Add a Storage class that writes the
whole list to a text file whenever a command changes it.

Task gains an abstract toFileString() that each subclass implements, so
Storage never has to test a task's runtime type to decide which fields
to write. The path is built with java.nio.file.Path rather than string
concatenation, so no separator is hardcoded, and the parent directory
is created on demand.

The save file itself is gitignored; it is user data, not source.

Saving was only half of the feature: the file was written but never
read back, so a restarted GOAT still began with an empty list.

Add Storage.load(), which decodes each line into the right Task
subclass and restores its done flag. A missing file is treated as a
first run rather than an error, so the empty case needs no special
handling by the caller.

Clear the data directory at the start of runtest.sh. Now that tasks
survive between runs, the previous run's file would otherwise be
loaded and the output would no longer match EXPECTED.TXT.

commitResults.messageTitle: Handle missing and malformed save files
commitResults.messageBody:
The decoder trusted the file completely. A line with too few fields
threw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, and an unrecognised type letter
fell through to the Event branch, so a damaged line was silently turned
into the wrong kind of task.

Validate every field before use and reject anything unexpected: a bad
type letter, a status other than 0 or 1, a blank required field, or a
line too short for its type. Bad lines are counted and skipped rather
than aborting the load, so one damaged line no longer costs the user
the rest of their list, and GOAT reports how many it skipped.

An unreadable file and a failed write are both reported and survived,
leaving GOAT usable rather than refusing to start.

A deadline stored its due date as free text, so GOAT could display it
but could not compare or reason about it, and a typo like 2019-13-45
was accepted as happily as a real date.

Store the due date as a java.time.LocalDate. Add a DateFormats helper
that reads the ISO form yyyy-mm-dd for both user input and save-file
fields, and renders MMM dd yyyy for display. Keeping the stored form
separate from the displayed form means the file stays machine-readable
however the display later changes, and a date round-trips through the
exact format it was written in.

Invalid dates are reported with the expected format rather than
crashing.

Events kept their start and end as free text, so the two halves of a
period could not be compared and an event could be created that ended
before it began.

Store both endpoints as LocalDate, reusing the DateFormats helper added
for deadlines, and reject an end date earlier than the start. Add
occursOn(), which asks whether an event is running on a given date and
is the basis for querying by date.

A save file written before this change holds free text where a date is
now expected. Those lines fail to decode and are skipped by the
existing corrupt-line handling, so an old file costs the user only the
dated tasks rather than preventing GOAT from starting.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add on command to list tasks by date
commitResults.messageBody:
Storing dates as LocalDate is only worth doing if something asks
questions of them. Add an "on <date>" command that lists the deadlines
due on a date and the events running across it, which is the first
feature that could not have been written while dates were free text.

Deadlines match by equality and events by falling within their span,
endpoints included. To-dos carry no date and never match.

The command list quoted back on unrecognised input is generated from
the Command enum, so it picked up the new keyword without being
edited.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract Ui class for user interaction
commitResults.messageBody:
GOAT mixed three unrelated jobs in one class: talking to the user,
deciding what a command means, and managing the task list. Separating
them starts with the most self-contained of the three.

Move the banner, the bot name, the horizontal rule, the reply
formatting and the input Scanner into a Ui class. GOAT now asks Ui for
the next command and hands it messages to display, and no longer
mentions System.out or Scanner at all.

The gain is that the wording, the indentation and the rules can change
without touching command logic, and a future interface that is not a
terminal would replace Ui rather than being threaded through GOAT.

Behaviour is unchanged: the text UI test passes against the existing
expected output without re-blessing.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract TaskList to own the task collection
commitResults.messageBody:
GOAT held the ArrayList directly and reached into it from every command
handler, so the collection had no owner and no place to put operations
that belong to the list as a whole.

Move the collection into a TaskList class exposing add, delete, get,
size, isEmpty and findOn. TaskList does no printing and no saving: it
answers questions and changes tasks, leaving the caller to decide what
to say and when to write to disk. That keeps it testable without a
terminal or a file, which matters for the JUnit increment.

Replace the instanceof chain behind the "on" command with an occursOn
method on Task, overridden by Deadline and Event. Asking each task
whether it matches removes the need for any caller to test a task's
runtime type, and a future dated task type would work without editing
the query.

Narrow Storage.load() to return List rather than ArrayList, so callers
depend on the interface rather than the implementation.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract Parser to interpret user commands
commitResults.messageBody:
Working out what the user meant was spread through GOAT: the main loop
split the line by hand, and four parseX methods sat among the command
handlers they served.

Move all of it into a Parser class returning a ParsedCommand record of
the command and its arguments. GOAT's loop now reads a line, asks
Parser what it means, and dispatches, with no string handling of its
own.

Split the task-number check across the boundary it actually falls on.
Parser answers whether a number was given and whether it is a number,
which it can judge from the text alone. Whether that number refers to
an existing task depends on the list, so GOAT keeps that check in a new
toIndex method. Parsing therefore needs no knowledge of the task list,
which is what makes it testable in isolation.

Error messages and their order are unchanged, verified against the
existing expected output without re-blessing.

commitResults.messageTitle: Convert GOAT to an instance with injected collaborators
commitResults.messageBody:
GOAT was a bag of static methods sharing static state, so its
collaborators could not be substituted and the save path was fixed at
compile time.

Give GOAT a constructor taking the save file path and holding Ui,
Storage and TaskList as fields, with main() reduced to constructing one
and calling run(). The path is now a parameter, so a test or a second
instance can point at a different file.

Loading happens in the constructor but its outcome is reported at the
start of run(), so the greeting still comes before any complaint about
the save file. Being shown an error before GOAT has said hello reads
badly, and holding the message costs one field.

Behaviour is unchanged: persistence, date handling, the on command and
corrupt-file recovery were each re-checked, and the text UI test passes
without re-blessing.

commitResults.messageTitle: Organise classes into packages under seedu.goat
commitResults.messageBody:
All twelve classes sat in the default package, so nothing in the file
tree showed how they relate and every class was visible to every other
one.

Move them into seedu.goat with command, parser, storage, task and ui
subpackages, matching the layers separated during A-MoreOOP. Package
boundaries now make the intended dependencies explicit: the parser
imports from task because it builds tasks, while task imports nothing
from parser.

GoatException and DateFormats stay at the root because all three layers
use them; burying either inside one subpackage would force the others
to import across for no reason.

Rename GOAT to Goat and GOATException to GoatException. Java treats
acronyms in type names as ordinary words, and doing it now costs
nothing because every file is moving anyway. The bot still calls itself
GOAT when greeting the user; only the type names changed.

Update runtest.sh and the README for the new entry point,
seedu.goat.Goat. The files were moved with git mv, so history follows
them.

commitResults.messageTitle: Point the Gradle build at the Goat main class
commitResults.messageBody:
The build file merged from add-gradle-support is written for the
unmodified template, so it names seedu.duke.Duke as the application
main class and duke.jar as the shadow jar output. Neither exists in
this project.

Set mainClass to seedu.goat.Goat and the shadow jar name to goat.jar,
so gradlew run launches the chatbot and the assembled jar is named
after it.

Document both gradlew run and gradlew build in the README, noting that
the wrapper removes any need to install Gradle.

Verified: gradlew build succeeds and gradlew run drives the chatbot
through adding, listing and exiting. Build output stays out of git,
which .gitignore already covered.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for parsing, storage and the task list
commitResults.messageBody:
The only automated check was the text UI test, which drives the whole
program through stdin. That catches regressions in the finished output
but says nothing about which unit broke, and it cannot reach cases such
as a save file damaged in a particular way.

Add 54 JUnit 5 tests across four classes, mirroring the main package
structure under src/test/java. The three targets are the ones where a
bug would be quiet rather than obvious:

- Parser, tested with nothing but strings because it deliberately has
  no dependency on the task list.
- Storage, tested inside a JUnit temporary directory so the real save
  file is never touched, covering the round trip and each way a line
  can be malformed.
- TaskList and DateFormats, covering the event span endpoints and the
  boundary between the stored and displayed date forms.

Cases are named featureUnderTest_scenario_expectedBehavior. Several
guard bugs that were actually present earlier, such as an unknown type
letter in the save file being decoded as some other kind of task.

The suite was checked by mutation rather than by assuming: excluding
the endpoints from an event span makes two tests fail, so they are
testing behaviour rather than restating the implementation.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document building and running the JAR

commitResults.messageBody:
Classes and methods were already documented as they were written, so
this increment fills the two gaps that were left.

Add package-info.java for all six packages. Package documentation is
the one level Javadoc offers that this project had nothing at, and it
is the natural place to record why a package exists and what it may
depend on, which no single class can state.

Document each constant of the Command enum. Enum constants are public
members and were reported as undocumented by the javadoc tool, which
found nine gaps that reading the code for missing comment blocks had
missed.

gradlew javadoc now completes with no warnings, so the documentation is
checked by a tool rather than by inspection.

commitResults.messageTitle: Enforce the project Java coding standard with Checkstyle
commitResults.messageBody:
The code broadly followed the se-education intermediate standard
already, but compliance rested on inspection and nothing stopped it
drifting.

Fix the two naming rules the code actually broke. Rename occursOn to
isOn, because the standard requires boolean methods to read as is, has
or was. Rename Command.keyword to getKeyword, because method names must
be verbs and a bare noun does not read as one.

Add Checkstyle to the build, configured to the rules from that standard
a tool can decide: no tabs, a 120 character limit, explicit imports in a
fixed group order, braces on every conditional and loop, no public
fields, one statement per line, array specifiers on the type, and
Javadoc on types and public methods.

Test sources get their own configuration, because the standard requires
the underscored featureUnderTest_testScenario_expectedBehavior form for
test methods and exempts test code from the Javadoc rule. A single
configuration cannot express both.

Checkstyle runs as part of gradlew build and both source sets pass. The
configuration was checked by introducing a violation, which failed the
build as intended.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add find command to search tasks by keyword
commitResults.messageBody:
A list that only grows becomes hard to use: once it holds more than a
screenful, the only way to locate a task is to read all of them.

Add "find <keyword>", which lists the tasks whose description contains
the keyword. Matching is case insensitive, because a user searching for
a word should not have to remember how they capitalised it when adding
the task, and it matches within words so that searching for book finds
a bookshop.

The match is decided by Task.hasKeyword rather than by TaskList reading
the description, keeping the description private to the task and the
search free of any knowledge of the task types, as the date query
already is.

Only the description is searched. A deadline due in October is not a
match for "Oct", which would otherwise surprise a user searching for a
word they typed.

Add ten tests covering the matching rules and the missing-keyword
error, and extend the text UI test with the new command.

# Conflicts:
#	src/main/java/seedu/goat/command/Command.java

commitResults.messageTitle: Return replies as text instead of printing them
commitResults.messageBody:
Every command handler in Goat now builds its reply and returns it, and Ui
prints whatever it is handed. Previously the handlers called ui.show()
themselves, which tied the command logic to standard output and left no way
to obtain a reply without printing it.

Splitting the two apart is what makes a second interface possible: a window
can call getResponse() for the same text the text interface prints, without
inheriting the horizontal rules and indentation that only suit a terminal.
Ui keeps the varargs show(), now splitting each message on its newlines so a
reply built elsewhere as one block is still indented line by line.

The parting message moves into Goat because it is part of the conversation
rather than part of the presentation. It is returned by the bye command and
also printed when input runs out beforehand, so a piped file signs off the
same way a typed session does. text-ui-test output is unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a JavaFX window for the chatbot
commitResults.messageBody:
GOAT now opens a chat window in which the user's messages and GOAT's replies
appear as bubbles on opposite sides, each beside an avatar. The layout lives
in FXML and the colours in CSS, so the arrangement and the appearance of the
window can both be changed without recompiling anything.

The window holds no task logic of its own. It passes what was typed to
Goat.getResponse() and shows whatever comes back, which is the same text the
text interface prints, so the two interfaces cannot disagree about what a
command does. Both share the save file, so a list built in one is there in
the other.

Launcher exists because launching an Application subclass directly makes the
JVM require the JavaFX modules on the module path, which fails once the
shadow JAR puts them on the classpath instead. Starting from a plain class
sidesteps that.

The build declares the JavaFX artifacts for Windows, macOS and Linux rather
than only this machine's, following the sample build.gradle in the course's
JavaFX tutorial, so the JAR is not tied to the platform it was built on and
does not depend on the JDK happening to bundle JavaFX. runtest.sh now
compiles through Gradle for the same reason: plain javac can no longer find
the JavaFX classes. Its output is unchanged.

A bye disables the input controls and closes the window a moment later,
rather than at once, so the goodbye can be read before it disappears.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use varargs where a caller knows its arguments up front
commitResults.messageBody:
Two places take varargs now, both where the caller writes its arguments out
literally and had to work around not being able to.

TaskList's no-argument constructor becomes TaskList(Task...), so a caller
that already knows its tasks can name them in place instead of building an
empty list and calling add() once per task. Most of TaskListTest was doing
exactly that, and reads better for the change. new TaskList() still compiles
and still means an empty list, because no arguments is a valid varargs call.
The List constructor stays for Storage, which loads a list whose length is
not known when the code is written and so gains nothing from varargs.

Goat.reply(String...) replaces the repeated String.join("\n", ...) calls the
GUI increment left behind. Naming the operation says what those lines are
rather than how they are stuck together. Replies whose length depends on the
task list still build a list and join it, since varargs would buy them
nothing there.

Ui.show(String...) was already varargs and is unchanged.
